text:
M.R. c. K.M.

2008 QCCS 3545

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-14-028568-079

DATE:

July 29, 2008

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

LOUIS-PAUL CULLEN, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

M. R.

and

S. R.

Petitioners

and

D.
R.

Reasonable Person

v.

K. M.

Respondent

and

MA. R.

and

THE PUBLIC
CURATOR FOR QUEBEC

Mises en cause

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

I- THE DISPUTE

[
1
]

The Petitioners are the son and daughter of the
late So. R. and of Respondent K. M..  They seek the opening of a regime of
protective supervision for their mother and an order for her medical
examination.

[
2
]

Their sister Ma. R. and their mother oppose the
motion, as does Mr. D. R., Mrs. K. R.'s son-in-law described in the style of
cause as a "Reasonable Person".

[
3
]

Mr. R. expresses his opposition to the motion in
a brief affidavit dated May 29, 2008 where he states that Mrs. K. R.
"possesses all of her mental capacities", without providing any
factual basis in support of this opinion.

II- PROCEDURAL ISSUES

[
4
]

On March 7, 2007, judge Richer ordered Mrs. K.
R. to undergo a geriatric and psychosocial examination and ordered Mrs. R. to
refrain from interfering "in any manner whatsoever", such as advising
her mother not to cooperate with such an examination.

[
5
]

On June 11, 2008, less than a week before the
beginning of the hearing which had been scheduled on September 10, 2007 for
five days commencing June 16, 2008, counsel jointly representing Mrs. K. R. and
Mrs. R. filed a notice of production of an undated expert report signed by Dr.
Ruby Friedman, M.D., Associate Director, Division of Geriatric Medecine, Jewish
General Hospital.

[
6
]

This report, titled "Geriatric and
Cognitive Assessment", pertains to an assessment of Mrs. K. R. conducted
on June 5 and 6, 2008 in the presence, on both occasions, of Mrs. R..

[
7
]

At the outset of the hearing, Petitioners'
counsel requested an immediate postponement by reason of the late filing of Dr.
Friedman's report.

[
8
]

In order to decide whether this was in the best
interest of Mrs. K. R., the Court allowed the Petitioners as well as Mrs. R. to
address the matter.

[
9
]

The Court was also provided with transcripts of
the hearing before judge Richer on March 5 and 7, 2007.

[
10
]

In addition to the material contained in the
court file, the Court was further provided with the following documents:

-

Transcript of the judgment rendered orally on
December 22, 2004 by judge Gagnon in file no. 500-14-022564-041 denying Mrs. R.
motion to probate the draft will of the late So. R..  According to the court's
computerized records, there were no further proceedings in that file.

-

Key pleadings in file no. 500-17-025176-051,
where M. R., his sister S. and their brother D. (represented by his
daughter/Curatrix) are seeking a declaration that Mrs. R. is unworthy to
inherit her share in the succession of the late So. R. and damages totalling
$600,000.  As cross-plaintiff, Mrs. R. is asking the court, in particular, to
declare that her siblings have renounced their father's succession, are
unworthy to inherit, to order various accountings, to condemn them to pay her
damages of $650,000 and to declare that her own children are called to the
succession in her stead.

-

Key pleadings in file no. 500-17-025385-058,
where S. R. and [Company A] are suing [Company B] for a declaration that S. R.
is the owner of the property located at [...], Town A.

[
11
]

In May 2008, judge Corriveau heard cases no.
500-17-025176-051 and no.                               500-17-025385-058 and
took them under advisement.

[
12
]

As of June 2008, Mrs. K. R. had not yet
undergone a psychosocial examination, contrary to judge Richer's order.

[
13
]

After the Court had questioned Mrs. K. R. at her
residence, the Petitioners dropped their request for a postponement.

[
14
]

On June 18, 2008, the parties consented to
several safeguard orders until the date of the judgment to be rendered on the
merits of the motion for protective supervision and medical examination:

-

Mrs. K. R. was to undergo a psychosocial
examination regarding the effect of her diverse anxieties on her capacity to
take care of herself and to administer her property as well as on the
appropriate treatment or therapy for her difficulty with swallowing.

-

Mrs. R. was to refrain from any communications
whatsoever with the personnel participating in this examination and not to be
present at any meeting between such personnel and her mother.

-

Mrs. K. R. was not to give away any money or
transfer any property to her children.

[
15
]

The parties agreed that the hearing would be
completed during the last week of July 2008, upon filing of the appropriate
psychosocial examination report, the testimony of their author(s) and argument.

[
16
]

Mrs. K. R.'s psychosocial examination was not
carried out, as Mrs. R. and her mother opposed the selection of the expert, an
associate professor of psychiatry at McGill University and senior psychiatrist
at the Jewish General Hospital.

[
17
]

The hearing resumed on July 28, 2008.

[
18
]

Counsel for Mrs. K. R. and Mrs. R. sought
immediate leave to cease representing their clients.

[
19
]

Mrs. R. confirmed that she and her mother intended to instruct their
future counsel to oppose the Petitioners' motion for
protective supervision and medical examination.

[
20
]

The Petitioners' counsel did not insist on a psychosocial examination,
conceding that it could hardly be fruitful without Mrs. K. R.'s cooperation.

[
21
]

The matter at issue being of public order, the Court ordered
counsel for Mrs. K. R. and Mrs. R. to proceed on the basis that their
instructions were to oppose the Petitioners' motion.

III- THE FACTS

[
22
]

Mrs. K. R. is 77 years old.  Of her immediate
family, she alone survived Auschwitz.

[
23
]

She married Mr. So. R. in the late forties.

[
24
]

Their marriage produced four children: D. R.,
the eldest, is 56.  His daughter is his Curatrix.  M. R. is 52.  Mrs. R. is 48,
is married and has four children aged 7, 11, 15 and 17.  S. R., is 35.

[
25
]

Mrs. K. R.'s four children all reside in the
Province of Quebec, although Mrs. R.'s main residence is in the State of New
York where her two oldest children, still minors, are living.

[
26
]

Soon after Mr. So. R. passed away in June 2003,
his children began their legal battles, initially over the probate of a draft
will.

[
27
]

That conflict ended in December 2004, when
judge Gagnon dismissed Mrs. R.'s motion to probate the draft will, having
found, on the balance of probabilities, that it had not been witnessed,
contrary to what she was alleging.

[
28
]

As a result, one third of Mr. So. R.'s assets
were to be distributed to his widow and the remainder to their four children.

[
29
]

More legal battles quickly ensued between the
children.

[
30
]

Mrs. K. R.'s condition took a turn for the worse
in November 2006 when hearing dates were set for the trials between her
children in cases                      no. 500-17-025176-051 and no.
500-17-025385-058.

[
31
]

When Mrs. K. R. was admitted to the Jewish
General Hospital in November 2006, her anxiousness was such that she no longer
could bring herself to eat.  She feared that she would choke if she tried to
swallow.

[
32
]

On a date in November 2006 that she says she
cannot recall, Mrs. R. left her home in the State of New York as well as her
husband and four minor children to be with her mother in Town A.

[
33
]

On November 13, 2006, Mrs. K. R. signed a power
of attorney in favour of Mrs. R..

[
34
]

On December 1
st
, 2006, Mrs. K. R.
signed another power of attorney in favour of Mrs. R., specifically to conduct
her banking affairs at the Royal Bank of Canada.

[
35
]

On December 13, 2006, Mrs. K. R. signed a third
power of attorney in favour of Mrs. R..  This document appointed Mrs. R.'s
husband, a real-estate lawyer practicing in the State of New York, to replace
her daughter, if necessary.

[
36
]

These powers of attorney were intended to ensure
Mrs. R. that the Petitioners, to whom she icily refers as her
"siblings" and with whom she was already engaged in litigation, would
not interfere with her actions.

[
37
]

Mrs. K. R. was readmitted to the Jewish General
Hospital from January to April 2007 and, after considerable weight loss, a
feeding tube was inserted and her weight was stabilized.

[
38
]

Mrs. R. continues to reside with her mother,
although rotating personnel attends to the latter's needs around-the-clock,
seven days a week.

[
39
]

Mrs. R.'s two youngest children have also moved
in with them.

IV- ANALYSIS

[
40
]

The Petitioners allege that Mrs. R. influenced
their mother before and during her hospitalizations to refuse to cooperate with
the geriatric evaluation that her condition necessitated and interfered with
their mother's treatment while she was hospitalized.

[
41
]

They add that Mrs. R. has taken control of their
mother to the exclusion of the other members of the family and express their
fear that Mrs. R. has been given free rein to dispose of their mother's assets.

[
42
]

The Petitioners further allege that Mrs. K. R.
is vulnerable, severely incapacitated and lacking in judgment and that the
opening of a regime of protective supervision is required in her interest.

Mrs. R.'s conduct

[
43
]

The Petitioners' concerns with respect to Mrs.
R.'s conduct are not merely conjectural.

[
44
]

In March 2007, before judge Richer, Dr. Luc
Trudeau of the Jewish General Hospital made it plain that Mrs. R. had
interfered with the medical team to the extent that, on one occasion, she had
to be evacuated to another floor by security guards.

[
45
]

In her testimony before this Court, Mrs. R.
acknowledged "tension" between herself and the physicians at the
Jewish General Hospital.  She claimed that they had denied her mother all
medication.

[
46
]

In reality, it is plain from Dr. Michelle
Elizoff's affidavit of February 28, 2007 and Dr. Trudeau's testimony that Mrs.
R. actually prevented her mother from taking medication prescribed to her.

[
47
]

Moreover, Mrs. R. administered medication to her
mother that had not been prescribed.

[
48
]

Mrs. R.'s interference with her mother's
physicians was dangerously misguided and, in their opinion, put her mother's
health at risk.

[
49
]

Mrs. R. denies any responsibility for her
actions and goes so far as to contend that the physicians "tortured"
her mother, which is hardly believable.

[
50
]

Mrs. R. states that she would stop at nothing to
protect her mother.  The Court believes that this statement equally applies to
her determination to protect her self-interest.

[
51
]

Her decision to reside with her mother in
November 2006 was not solely motivated by a genuine interest in her mother's
well being.  It was inspired by the desire to protect from the Petitioners what
she considers to be her fair share of her father's assets.

[
52
]

Mrs. R.'s conduct during the course of the
present proceedings has been questionable.

[
53
]

On March 7, 2007, as already noted, judge Richer
ordered Mrs. K. R. to undergo a geriatric and psychosocial examination at the
Jewish General Hospital, under the supervision of the medical personnel at the
geriatric department and further ordered Mrs. R. to refrain from interfering in
any manner whatsoever with the aforesaid medical and psychological examination
and specifically to refrain from advising her mother not to cooperate with such
an examination.

[
54
]

As already noted, Mrs. K. R. geriatric
assessment was not arranged until June 2008, fifteen months after judge
Richer's order, less than one week before the hearing.

[
55
]

According to Dr. Friedman, Mrs. R. did not
"interfere" with his geriatric assessment.

[
56
]

Mrs. R. did provide him with part of her
mother's medical history, including inaccurate information concerning the site
of an infection.  In addition, Mrs. R.'s mere presence during the assessment
may have influenced some of her mother's answers.

[
57
]

Dr. Friedman considers that his assessment also
serves as a "psychosocial examination".

[
58
]

The Court disagrees.

[
59
]

Dr. Friedman did not have access to Mrs. K. R.'s
complete medical file (which was in the process of being digitalized).  He did
not discuss her anxieties with respect to eating, sleeping alone, leaving her
house, choking or dying.  He did not consider the significance of the diagnosed
psychological disorder that still prevents her from eating or drinking
normally.

[
60
]

No valid reason was offered to explain the
failure by Mrs. R. and her mother to cooperate with the latter's psychosocial
assessment ordered in June 2008.

[
61
]

In short, Mrs. R.'s improper behaviour and continued
lack of judgment with respect to the care of her mother combined with her keen
interest in her father's succession raise objective concerns over the
possibility of conflicting interests with her mother regarding her mother's
care and the administration of her property.

[
62
]

Bearing this in mind, the central issue remains
whether Mrs. K. R. is presently incapable of making her own decisions regarding
her person or her property.

Mrs. K. R.'s present capacity

[
63
]

Prior to the orders rendered by judge Richer in March 2007, Mrs. K. R.'s
health as well as her refusals to cooperate with her treating physicians and
follow their advice raised serious concerns.

[
64
]

Mrs. K. R.'s capacity to make informed decisions regarding her own
health was questioned during her hospitalization at the Jewish General Hospital
in early 2007:

-

Luc Trudeau, M.D., a physician practicing in internal medicine,
testified in March 2007 that Mrs. K. R. had refused to cooperate with
investigations of her condition, that she had lost all autonomy, that her
extreme anxiety levels were preventing her from eating normally and, that under
the influence of Mrs. R., she was making decisions that
were endangering her health.

-

Karl Looper, M.D., deplored in April 2007 Mrs. K. R.'s lack of
cooperation with her psychosocial assessment.  He acknowledged that she was not
"globally incompetent", but did question her appreciation of her
medical situation as well as her judgment in refusing to cooperate with her
care.

[
65
]

Mrs. K. R.'s situation has since improved considerably. She lives at
home in the constant care of attendants under conditions of which she appears
to be satisfied.

[
66
]

She remains quite frail and physically vulnerable.  Her autonomy is
reduced and she still suffers from anxieties that prevent her from ingesting
food otherwise than through a feeding tube inserted into her body, but this
disorder no longer threatens her existence.

[
67
]

The evidence shows that since Mrs. K. R.'s discharge from hospital in
the Spring of 2007, she has been mentally competent to make her own decisions:

-

Psychological assessment dated May 18, 2007 by psychologist
Nathan Kuperstok, Ph. D., based on meetings with Mrs. K. R. on May 9, 10 and
13, 2007;

-

Geriatric and Cognitive Assessment, undated, by Ruby Friedman,
M.D., based on meetings with Mrs. K. R. on June 5 and 6, 2008;

[
68
]

This accords with the Court's own observations in June 2008.  In the presence of the court clerk, the Court questioned Mrs. K. R.
at her residence during approximately one and one half hours.

[
69
]

While noting Mrs. K. R.'s obvious emotional
disturbance over her children's quarrels, the Court was impressed with her
overall clarity of mind.

[
70
]

Mrs. K. R. stated and explained the following:

-

She loves her children equally and believes they
are fighting over her property.

-

She is distraught by their legal proceedings.
She never made a will.

-

Children must care for their parents.  Mrs. R.
is the only one of her children who is available and willing to care for her.
She wishes for this to continue.

-

Mrs. R. asks her to sign checks.  Mrs. K. R.
claims that she personally verifies her own monthly bank reports, but does not
know how much money she needs to pay her monthly expenses.

-

Mrs. R. is not paid a salary, but since November
2006, Mrs. K. R. has allowed her to withdraw $200,000 from a checking account
and to transfer in her name a property situated in Florida, which Mrs. K. R.
values at $90,000.

-

She expresses no criticism whatsoever toward her
son D., Mrs. R. or her late husband, but sharply criticises her other daughter,
her son-in-law and her son M. regarding material things and their lack of
concern for her.

-

She does not want her children nor the Public
Curator to administer her finances, and she wishes to stay in her home as long
as possible rather than move into a retirement home.

[
71
]

Her cognitive abilities are not substantially impaired.  She understands
her condition, knows what she wants and expresses her desires strongly and
clearly.

[
72
]

Above all, she wishes to remain in full control of her destiny.

[
73
]

She has no desire to improve her health at the risk of jeopardizing her
current arrangement with Mrs. R. or of being removed
from her residence.  Hence, her continuing resistance to cooperate with a
psychosocial examination.

[
74
]

The Petitioners argue, in essence, that Mrs. K. R.'s incapacity is
demonstrated by the fact that her decisions are not in her best interest.

[
75
]

Although some of Mrs. K. R.'s decisions are objectively disputable, they
are her decisions to make: she is not in any danger from her current medical
condition and is fully able to weight the benefits as well as the drawbacks of
her current situation, including her arrangement with Mrs. R..

[
76
]

Mrs. K. R.'s capacity extends to deciding whether to consent to or to
refuse care and choosing whether to follow the advice of Mrs. R. despite the
latter's poor judgment and despite some apparent conflict between their
respective interests.

[
77
]

Pursuant to article 10 and following of the
Civil Code of Quebec
,
no person of full age and of sound mind may be made to undergo care of any
nature except with his or her consent.

[
78
]

A person's refusal to undergo care is not, in and of itself, conclusive
with respect to his or her incapacity to make an informed decision in this
respect.

[
79
]

Pursuant to art. 258
C.C.Q.
, protective supervision of a person
of full age is ordered where such a person is incapable to care for himself or
herself or to administer his or her property

(…) by reason, in particular, of illness, deficiency
or debility due to age which impairs the person's mental faculties or physical
ability to express his or her will.

[
80
]

Mrs. K. R. mental faculties are neither deficient nor debilitated and
she remains physically able to express her will, which is unquestionably to
maintain her situation as it presently is, for as long as possible.

[
81
]

The imposition of protective supervision in favor of a person of full
age requires cogent evidence, for it restricts the future exercise of his or
her legal rights.

[
82
]

In the case at hand, the Petitioners have not discharged their burden of
proving that Mrs. K. R. is mentally incompetent to make decisions regarding her
care or the administration of her property.

[
83
]

Their motion will accordingly be dismissed.

[
84
]

Mrs. R. did not offer any explanation why her mother, while in her care,
did not submit to a psychosocial examination despite the court orders of March
7, 2007 and June 18, 2008, nor why Dr. Friedman's cognitive assessment was
performed so late and so close to the dates set for the hearing in June 2008.

[
85
]

Costs on the motion will therefore be awarded against Mrs. R..

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

DISMISSES
the
"Amended motion for the institution of protective supervision of a person
of full age and to obtain an order for a medical examination", with costs
against Mrs. R..
